learning_objective: 🎯 Journey back in time to understand how early humans used cave walls as their canvas to document hunting, dancing, and their daily lives!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Art created before the invention of writing. Early humans painted on cave walls to express themselves, record events, or possibly for magical/religious rituals related to hunting.
The earliest paintings. They are linear, mostly in dark red and green, featuring huge animal figures like bisons, elephants, and tigers. Green was used for dancers and red for hunters.

The largest number of paintings belong to this era. The size of figures became smaller. Hunting scenes dominate, showing people with spears, bows, and arrows. We also see family life, dancing, and pregnant animals.
The Copper Age. Paintings here show the transition to agriculture. You see people riding horses and elephants, using pottery, and trading with other communities.

Located in Madhya Pradesh, discovered by V.S. Wakankar in 1957. It has over 800 rock shelters, with 500 bearing paintings. The artists used natural minerals like Hematite (Geru) for red and Chalcedony for green.

fun_activity.title: 🎨 Natural Pigment Painting
fun_activity.instructions: Try painting like a caveman! Grind some turmeric (yellow), charcoal/soot (black), and red clay or brick dust (red). Mix them with a little water and tree sap (or glue). Use twigs or your fingers to paint a hunting scene on a rough stone!

exam_tips: 📌 Bhimbetka is a guaranteed topic. Memorize its location (M.P.), discoverer (V.S. Wakankar, 1957-58), and the main colors used (Red and White).
📌 Differentiate the periods: Paleolithic (large, linear animals), Mesolithic (smaller, dynamic hunting scenes, human activities).
📌 Remember how they made colors: grinding mineral rocks (like hematite for red) and mixing them with animal fat or plant sap.
quick_recap: ⭐ The subjects of these paintings were everyday life: hunting, dancing, and animal figures.
⭐ Red (geru) and white were the most universally used colors.
⭐ Prehistoric artists often painted over older paintings, sometimes leaving up to 20 layers of art on a single rock wall!
